content.summary_of_the_paper: Regular supervised pretraining on ImageNet has poor transferability on downstream datasets, due to the excess intra-class clustering that ignores the information within the class. The authors propose RenyiSCL, maximizing the Renyi divergence between different classes instead of optimizing the cross-entropy or contrastive loss between classes. The authors find that RenyiSCL helps improve the transferability by easy-positive mining, i.e., putting low weight on the hard positive samples to prevent losing its discriminating information that may benefit downstream tasks. The authors also propose to set different mining strategy for classes with different frequencies, trading off between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance. Experiments are conducted on transfer learning and class-imbalanced dataset, showing the effectiveness of RenyiSCL.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ The motivation is sensible and the intuition is clear.

+ Setting different $\lambda$ for different classes is a clean way to increase transferability while preserving the generalizaiton.

- The authors use linear probing to evaluate on downstream datasets. I wonder if the superiority of RenyiSCL still holds if we evaluate by finetuning the whole network. In this case, finetuning may restore the crucial information in downstream datasets that is ignored during pretraining, improving the transferability of models pretrained with cross-entropy or SupCon.

- In Table 7, I notice that when fixing $\lambda_{many}$ and $\lambda_{few}$, setting a smaller $\lambda_{med}$ will also lead to worse results on few-classes. Do you have any insight on this phenomenon? Intuitively, lower $\lambda$ should lead to better generalization and higher in-distribution results, but the numbers seem to indicate the opposite.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation is clear. The experiments are somewhat solid in that the authors test on many different downstream datasets. The method seems simple enough to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall the paper provides clear intuition on why supervised pretraining has poor transferability and how to address it, although I I think the results of finetuning on downstream datasets are also important for a full assessment of the algorithm.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fSzh
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer fSzh. 

We sincerely appreciate your effort in reviewing our manuscript. Here, we respond to your concerns as follows:

**Fine-tuning experiments**

While fine-tuning a network can further improve the performance of transfer learning, here we only consider the linear transfer experiments. This is because fine-tuning can dramatically distort the pretrained network for the target task thus, it cannot act as a measure to compare the quality of pre-trained representations. 

**Choosing hyperparameter**

We empirically find out that relative values of $\gamma$ are important in long-tailed recognition tasks. This is because $\gamma$ regulates not only intra-class variation but also the inter-class separation by hard negative mining. From our experiments, maintaining the large gap between $\gamma_{few}$ and $\gamma_{med}$ and $\gamma_{many}$ leads to the best generalization performance on a few samples, and if the gap becomes smaller, the generalization on a few samples group decreases.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose to apply the recently proposed Renyi Contrastive Learning of Lee & Shin to supervised learning (SL). It can be seen as a) RenyiCL when the positives and negatives are defined via labels or b) a generalization of SupCon when substituting for the loss function from Lee & Shin (RCL loss). Experiments show that this can boost transfer performance, while performance on the training tasks is similar to other SL methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strenghts 

S1: applying the RCL loss with labels boosts the transfer performance of RenyiCL. 

S2: the gamma parameter can be used for controlling the learning per class in an imbalanced learning setting

### Weaknesses

W1: **Unclear if the gains come from the loss change**.
The overall training setup between the proposed and compared methods is unclear: for example,  it is unclear where MC is used: LOOK, SupCon and SLMLP can all benefit from that. What is missing is a fair comparison, where everything else remains the same (MC, projector etc) and the only thing that changes is the loss function. SLMLP+MC is not in  Table 1 for example, neither is LOOK and when they are compared to it is in a comparisson that is not fair. Both SupCon and LOOK are very related to the proposed, and in fact Supcon is the same as the proposed with gamma=1. If I am not mistaken, performance of the proposed approach for gamma = 1 is missing, and even if it is somewhere to be found, it is not  very clearly and prominently presented. Both SupCon and LOOK are simple variants of the proposed setup that can be re-implemented for a fair comparison to see what the Renyi divergence brings. This weakness is further enhanced from the findings in Sariyildiz et all (2022) that show much higher absolute numbers with simply using cosine softmax, a projector and MC. The latter should also be cited and discussed. Finally, it is worth noting that with respect to the training task, RenyiSCL is outperformed by SupCon on Im1k.


W2: **Unclear insights/empirical novelty**.
It is to me unclear what insights this paper brings for the supervised case; a) What different isights we get using Remyi for the supervised case versus the self supervised one? For example, in 4.1 the authors say that they "show that RényiSCL performs intra-class easy positive and inter-class hard negative mining by controlling the hyperparameter γ." but this was also showin in RenyiCL. Then, the insight that gamma can control and help with imbalanced data is misguided given that it leads in practice to the same average perofrmanece, boosting "few" classes but hurting the rest.
Finally, there is no real insight on why is the supervised version of RCL RényiSCL better than RényiCL for transfer learning. Any intuitions on that? Cause to me it seems that this could come from other factors, ie te setups - Are the setups identical apart from the use of labels? does RényiCL in the Tables have Multi-crop and a projector head?


W3: **Minor technical novelty**.
In terms of technical novelty, this paper is taking the RCL contrastive loss, and sampling positives from labels, something that SupCon did a few years back for the InfoNCE loss. It is unclear to me what exactly is the technical contribution beyond that. 

W4: **Showing the effect of the gamma and alpha hyperparameters**.
It was hard for me to find a figure that shows the effect of alpha and gamma hyperparameters for the basic case, ie not the imbalanced one (did not check the full appendix carefully). Is this a way of controlling the "balance between generalization and transferability trade-off" cause if so this is missing. Moreover, gamma seems to be close to 1 in many cases, and as the authors say their loss function becomes the SupCon function in that case. Then, what is the real trend with gamma? how is performacne when gamma is equal to 1? 

W5: **Discussion with highly related works is missing**.
First, the method shares a lot of intuition with LOOK from Feng et al (2023), and as gamma increases, "the qθ assigns weights on only the closest instances of z", something similar to the LOOK loss. in fact, the motivation stated in the contributions that "obtain a more transferable representation by mitigating the class-collapse" has already been thoroughly discussed in LOOK that limits the positives to the clossest ones.
Second, the paper seems to share a lot of common intuitions and implementation details with the Sariyildiz et all (2022) paper without discussing or citing the work:  a) they share the discussion on "balance between generalization and transferability trade-off" (although this paper does not expand on nor show something that controls this balance); b) the use of cosine softmax with multi-crop (MC) and a projector (note that Sariyildiz et all (2022) use cosine softmax with a projector, while this is something that is __not__ borrowed from the SLMLP paper as the equation in 3.1 suggests)

W6: **missing comparisons/discussion for the coarse label case**.
The Grafit paper from Touvron  et al (2021) uses a contrastive loss for this task and is not cited nor discussed.

W7: **unclear if this helps in the imbalanced case**.
The effect of a different gamma for long-tail are practically non existent: performance on the tail classes increases but performance on the "many" and "med" classes decreases, with the average being unchanged (from Tab 7).


**References**

Sariyildiz et all (2022). Sariyildiz, Mert Bulent, et al. "Improving the Generalization of Supervised Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.15369 (2022).
Touvron  et al (2021). Touvron, Hugo, et al. "Grafit: Learning fine-grained image representations with coarse labels." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: See the section above for details. The paper is generally easy to read apart from where it matters: the loss function. Originality is low both in terms of technical novelty and empirical findings, while key questions arise on where the gains come from.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although possibly helpful, this version of the paper does not convince that there is merrit in using Renyi CL loss for the supervised case. Seeing how there are so many parts that need to be clarified, comparisons added and discussions to be added, I recommend rejection, but  I can see a better version of this paper with the proper discussions and empirical comparisons to be valuable if performance gains persist.

content.title: Response to Reviewer zPU6
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer zPU6.

We sincerely appreciate your effort in reviewing our manuscript. Here, we respond to your concerns as follows:

**Unclear if the gains come from the loss change** 

In Table 3 of our manuscript , we conduct a fair comparison with Exemplar v2, SLMLP and LOOK by discarding the usage of multi-crop in RenyiSCL, due to the computational issue in reproducing Exemplar v2 and LOOK with multi-crop. Also in Table 4 of our manuscript, we compare with SLMLP and SupCon (which is exactly the case when $\gamma=1$ of RenyiSCL) in both using and dropping multi-crop augmentation. Then, we have demonstrated the ascendancy of RenyiSCL in comparison with other supervised baseline. On the other hand, we were not aware of Trex [1], which is another strong supervised baseline. We appreciate the suggestion and will add the comparison with the Trex baseline! Thank you.

**Unclear insights/empirical novelty** 

Since RenyiCL is a self-supervised model, it does not take label information during training. Therefore, the easy positive sampling in RenyiCL and RenyiSCL differs that RenyiCL choose easy positives from the generated positive views, i.e., augmented data from the same image, therefore RenyiCL is used to enhance the robustness to the noisy view. On the other hand, RenyiSCL chooses easy positives from intra-class samples that increases the intra-class variability, and the intra-class variability is correlated with the transferability of representations. Empirically, RenyiCL and RenyiSCL both uses same architectural setup, e.g., same projection head and data augmentation, thus the superior performance of RenyiSCL is due to the wise usage of label information by choosing appropriate $\gamma$ for better intra-class variability.

**Minor technical novelty** 

RenyiSCL is a supervised version of RenyiCL, akin to SupCon that was made from InfoNCE loss. However, we highlight that the effect of easy positive sampling in RenyiSCL differs from RenyiCL that RenyiSCL conducts intra-class easy positive sampling which is not done in RenyiCL and SupCon, and it results in better transferability.
 
**Showing the effect of the gamma and alpha hyperparameters** 

Throughout the experiments, we choose $\gamma=2.0$ for ImageNet-1K and ImageNet coarse-to-fine learning tasks. Otherwise, we select $\gamma$ by validating on the validation set. In the case of $\gamma\rightarrow 1$, it is equivalent to SupCon. Remark that we do not consider $\alpha$ as a hyperparameter: we use $\alpha=1/C$, where $C$ is the number of classes. We will clarify the choice of hyperparameters until the end of the rebuttal period. 

**Missing related works**

We sincerely appreciate your constructive suggestions. We are going to add discussions on LOOK and T-Rex in our revised manuscripts. Remark that our method is similar to LOOK in that both methods focus more on local instances: LOOK does this by using kNN classifier and RenyiSCL does with easy positive sampling. The key difference is that LOOK selects easy positives in a manual way, i.e., by choosing k nearest neighbors, while RenyiSCL intrinsically selects easy positives with importance weights. Also, we found that T-Rex uses similar tactics to enhance transferability by using multi-crops and deeper projection head. To see the sole effect of RenyiSCL loss compared to T-Rex, we will add experiments using the same setup of T-Rex except the training loss. In addition, we are going to add Grafit [2] as related works in coarse-to-fine transfer learning.  
Lastly, as reviewer t4tR noticed, in SLMLP paper, they also demonstrated the effectiveness of using MLP in cosine cross-entropy loss. To reproduce SLMLP, we found out that cosine cross-entropy suits better in our experiments. We apologize for the misleading description, and we’ll revise it until the end of the rebuttal period.

**unclear if this helps in the imbalanced case** 

We would like to highlight that the RenyiSCL can dramatically enhance the performance on few-shot samples, which has been under-explored by other long-tailed recognition methods. Also, we would like to highlight that our method achieves the lowest gap between the accuracies of major and minor groups, which should be considered when training on the long-tailed datasets. Lastly, even though the overall performance lags behind by other methods, one can use ensemble methods (e.g., RIDE [3]) to boost the overall performance, which we leave for future direction. 


[1] Sariyildiz, Mert Bulent, et al. "Improving the Generalization of Supervised Models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.15369 (2022).

[2] Touvron, Hugo, et al. "Grafit: Learning fine-grained image representations with coarse labels." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.

[2] Wang, Xudong, et al. "Long-tailed recognition by routing diverse distribution-aware experts." arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.01809 (2020).

content.summary_of_the_paper: By breaking up the CE and SupCon losses, the authors explain the class collapse introduced by the $-z^T w_y$ term. An existing work RCL proposed a new objective for contrastive learning. Borrowing the loss from RCL, this work proposed supervised RCL. The major contributions are 1. Modified RCL objective applicable to the supervised domain. 2. Provided analysis regarding how RSCL can learn a transferable representation without class collapse. The proposed loss performs intra-class easy positive and inter-class hard negative mining by controlling the hyperparameter $\gamma$. The experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of the new objective.

However, modifying self-supervised loss and apply to the supervised problem is not something new. Also how to select the newly introduced hyperparameters and the robustness/generality of such hyperparameters is unclear.

Btw in Wang et al. (2022) Supervised Learning with MLP (SLMLP), where is the cosine cross-entropy used? Could you please clarify it?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a new loss function for supervised contrastive(SupCon) learning. Given a supervised set of images and class labels, supervised contrastive learning uses infoNCE loss in which the positives are taken from the samples from the same class as the query, and the negative set includes random samples from other classes. The representation learned by SupCon might not transfer properly compared to unsupervised infoNCE where the positives are simply taken from the positives, specifically when the classes are imbalanced. The method presented in this paper is a variation of SupCon based on Renyi contrastive learning that tries to find a proper compromise between generalization and transferability. The authors show promising results supporting their claims.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

- The paper conveys a clear and well-formulated message.
- It is well-written and easy to follow.
- The experimental set-up is well established.

Weaknesses: 
- From the shown results in the paper, the proposed method seems to sacrifice generalization for the sake of transferability. Namely, Table. 5 shows inconsistency in the performance in the case of the class imbalanced training set in transfer learning.

-  The methods require tuning $\gamma$ per class(or three values of $\gamma_{many}, \gamma_{med}, $\gamma_{few}$ ), which is cumbersome!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is almost clear (I have a question in the following), and Its quality is acceptable. It suffers from a lack of novelty to some extent, as it is built on the Reyni contrastive learning and SupCon. The authors provide enough details for reproducibility.

I have a question that the authors would be great to address particularly in their rebuttal:
You claim that when $\gamma \rightarrow 1$, RSCL is equivalent to the SupCon loss. Please note that there are two loss functions in the SupCon paper: $\mathcal{L}$-out (their Eq. 2) and $\mathcal{L}$-in (their Eq. 3). You are referring to their $\mathcal{L}$-out as SupCon loss. But with  $\gamma \rightarrow 1$, RSCL is equivalent to their $\mathcal{L}$-in, is it not?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I enjoyed reading this paper. It conveys a clear message, is well-written, and the experimental set-up is good. However, the performance is mixed; it requires more hyperparameter tuning. I would be happy to discuss more with the other reviewers and the authors for a better evaluation.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6048 by Reviewer LGfV

content.title: Response to the reviewer LGfV
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer LGfV.

We sincerely appreciate your inspiring review of our manuscript. For your question about the loss function, remark that the first-term of $\gamma$-RSCL loss is given as
$$
L_1 = \frac{1}{\gamma-1}\log \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \exp((\gamma-1) f(x,x_i^+)),
$$
therefore as $\gamma\rightarrow1$, it becomes $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x,x_i^+)$. 
For your information, the $L^{out}$ in SupCon [1] is given as

$$
L^{out} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \log \frac{\exp( f(x,x_i^+))}{\sum_{i=1}^N \exp(f(x,x_i^+)) + \sum_{j=1}^M \exp(f(x,x_j^-)) } = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N f(x,x_i^+) +\log (\sum_{i=1}^N \exp(f(x,x_i^+)) + \sum_{j=1}^M \exp(f(x,x_j^-)))
$$

Therefore, we would like to clarify that RSCL generalizes $L^{out}$ in SupCon paper rather than $L^{in}$.

[1] Khosla, Prannay, et al. "Supervised contrastive learning." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 18661-18673.
